title: Where You Go, I Will Go
subtitle: Ruth 1
description: A famine, three funerals in Moab, and a daughter-in-law who will not go home.
paragraphs: The book of Judges closed with a nation doing what was right in its own eyes, and this small book opens inside the same years, in the same small country, with a famine: "In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land." The famine reached Bethlehem, whose name means house of bread, and a man named Elimelech did what families did in famines all through Genesis. He took his wife Naomi and his two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, and crossed east into Moab to wait it out. Moab was not a neutral address. It was the nation born in a cave in Genesis 19, the nation of Balak and Balaam, the nation whose king Eglon had held Israel for eighteen years in the days of Ehud. Elimelech's family were Ephrathites of Bethlehem, Israelites of Judah, settling as sojourners among a people with a long history against their own.

In Moab, Elimelech died. His sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth, and the family stayed about ten years, long enough for a sojourn to become a life. Then both sons died as well, "and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband." The text piles the losses in one line and moves on, because Naomi is the one left holding them. A widow in a foreign country, with no sons, no grandchildren, and no claim on anyone, was as close to nothing as the ancient world had a category for. Everything she had carried into Moab was buried there.

What turned her toward home was news framed as a visitation: "When Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food, she and her daughters-in-law prepared to leave the land of Moab." It is worth noticing, here at the start, how this book handles God. He acts directly only twice in its four chapters, once here, giving His people food, and once at the very end. Everything between those two acts is people: their speeches, their choices, their kindnesses, with heaven mostly listening. Naomi heard that the famine at home had broken, and she set out on the road back to Judah with both her daughters-in-law beside her.

Partway along the road, she stopped and tried to send them home, and her farewell is the first sounding of the word this whole book is built on: "Go back, each of you to your mother’s home. May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me. May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." Loving devotion is the translation's phrase for the Hebrew word hesed, covenant kindness, loyalty that acts. Naomi blesses the young widows with the very thing they have shown her, and then releases them from her with a kiss. Both of them wept and refused: "Surely we will return with you to your people."

Naomi answered with arithmetic, and the arithmetic was merciless. "Return home, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands?" Even if she married that night and bore sons, would they wait, unmarried, for boys to grow up? The custom of a brother raising up heirs for the dead, which will drive the whole second half of this book, is here stated only to be ruled impossible. And under the arithmetic sat her verdict on herself: "it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She was not protecting them from a hard trip. She was telling them there was nothing at the end of it but her.

Orpah kissed her and went back, and the text holds no grudge against her for it; she did the sensible thing her mother-in-law had twice commanded. Ruth did something else. The verse says she clung to Naomi, and the Hebrew word is the Bible's word for a husband holding fast to his wife in Genesis. What she did next she did out loud, in the most famous speech in the book, spoken by a Moabite widow to an Israelite one on an open road: "Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me."

Every line of it is a door closing behind her. Not a visit, a relocation of existence: your road, your home, your people, your God, your grave. And she sealed it by swearing in the name of Naomi's God, the LORD, a God who was not hers by birth or by her people's worship, calling His judgment down on herself if she broke it. Naomi argued no further. "When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her." The two of them walked the rest of the way, down out of Moab's hills, across the Jordan valley, and up into Judah, mostly in silence, as far as the text is concerned. The book gives Ruth one great speech and then lets her be quiet for a long time.

Bethlehem noticed them come in. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women of the town exclaimed: "Can this be Naomi?" It had been more than ten years, and she had left with a husband and two sons and come back with a Moabite daughter-in-law and nothing else. Her answer to the town is the theological center of the chapter, and it is an accusation she makes against heaven with her chin up: "Do not call me Naomi," she replied. "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me." Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter. She was renaming herself after her losses and charging them, in public, to the account of the Almighty, and nobody in the town argued with her, and the narrator does not correct her either. The book lets her say it.

But the narrator does place one fact beside her speech, the way this book places all its hope, quietly and in passing. She had come back empty, she said, at the exact moment the harvest that feeds people was beginning, with Ruth standing next to her: "So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest." Full and empty are Naomi's words. The barley was God's timing, unannounced. What a penniless foreign widow could do in a town at barley harvest was go out to the fields, and that is where Ruth goes next, in the morning, to work.

title: As It Happened
subtitle: Ruth 2
description: A gleaner finds a field, a protector, and the first news of a redeemer.
paragraphs: Before Ruth takes a single step, the narrator introduces a man she has not met: "Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a prominent man of noble character from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz." Hold on to that description, a man of noble character. The book hands out that exact compliment twice, and the second time it will be Boaz saying it about Ruth. For now he is just a name in Elimelech's clan, a wealthy landowner in Bethlehem, and Ruth does not know he exists.

What Ruth knows is that two widows cannot eat a reputation, so the initiative in this chapter is entirely hers. "Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor." Gleaning was Israel's built-in mercy: the law Moses gave commanded harvesters to leave the edges of their fields unharvested and the dropped stalks where they fell, for the poor, for the foreigner, and for the widow. Ruth was all three at once. But the law gave gleaners a claim, not a welcome, and a lone foreign woman still needed a field owner in whose sight she found favor. Naomi's whole answer was permission and a blessing in four words: "Go ahead, my daughter," she replied.

"So Ruth departed and went out into the field and gleaned after the harvesters. And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech." She happened to come. The Hebrew piles chance on chance, her chance chanced upon his field, and the narrator lets the coincidence sit there smiling, in a book where God has acted directly exactly once and the characters pray constantly. Ruth chose a field at random, or thought she did, and it belonged to the one man in Bethlehem who was kin to her dead husband, wealthy enough to help, and, the day was about to show, the kind of man who noticed a stranger's daughter-in-law and asked questions about her.

Boaz came down from Bethlehem to his harvest, and the first words out of his mouth introduce him better than the narrator did: he greeted his harvesters: "The LORD be with you." And they answered in kind: "The LORD bless you," they replied. Then he saw the new gleaner and asked his foreman: "Whose young woman is this?" The foreman's answer identified her not by her name but by her story: "She is the Moabitess who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab." And he repeated her request from the morning, because it had stayed with him: "Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the harvesters." She had come at morning and worked straight through, he said, resting only a short time in the shelter. In a harvest field, in front of the owner, the foreman of Bethlehem testified to two things about the foreign widow: what she had done for Naomi, and how hard she worked.

Boaz went to her himself, and what he gave her was safety first and bread second. "Listen, my daughter. Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from this place, but stay here close to my servant girls." Stay with the women, he meant, and stay in my field, and the reason stands inside his next sentence: "Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled." A foreign widow gleaning alone in strange fields was exposed in ways the chapter does not need to spell out, because Naomi will spell them out tonight. Boaz removed the danger by command, gave her the run of the field, and put her on his own water jars like one of his workers.

Ruth went down on her face to the ground, and her question is the honest one underneath this whole book: "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?" Boaz's answer tells her that her story arrived in Bethlehem before she did, and he tells it back to her in vocabulary any Israelite would recognize: "I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and how you came to a people you did not know before." Left your father and your mother and the land of your birth. That is the shape of Abraham's call, Genesis 12, and Boaz uses it for a Moabite gleaner without blinking. Then he prayed over her, and his prayer is the seed of everything still coming: "May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge."

Ruth answered a woman who knew her place and planned to keep her dignity inside it: "My lord," she said, "may I continue to find favor in your eyes, for you have comforted and spoken kindly to your maidservant, though I am not like one of your servant girls." At mealtime he called her over, not to the gleaners' corner but beside the harvesters, bread and vinegar sauce and roasted grain pressed on her by the owner himself, and "she ate and was satisfied and had some left over." Satisfied is a word Bethlehem had not heard from this household since the famine. She saved the leftovers for Naomi without being told.

Then Boaz did the thing that separates generosity from manners. As she rose to glean again, he ordered his young men, out of her hearing: "Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her. Rather, pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather. Do not rebuke her." Gleaning was supposed to be scraps and leftovers, the economics of crumbs. Boaz quietly rewired it so his own harvesters were harvesting for her, dropping deliberate handfuls into her path and pretending it was accident. She gleaned until evening, beat out the grain, and carried home about an ephah of barley, a load no gleaner gathers in a day without help, plus the saved roasted grain from lunch.

Naomi saw the heap and did the math instantly. "Where did you glean today, and where did you work? Blessed be the man who noticed you." Ruth told her the name, and the older woman who had renamed herself Bitter three days before erupted in the book's second sounding of its great word: "May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead." Kindness is hesed again, the loving devotion Naomi had prayed over her daughters-in-law on the road, now appearing in a field owner's conduct. And then Naomi said the sentence that turns this chapter from a good day into a plot: "The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers." A kinsman-redeemer, a goel, was the family guardian in Israel's law, the relative charged with buying back a family's land before it was lost and rescuing kin who had fallen into ruin. Naomi had buried a husband and two sons and renamed herself for the bitterness of it, and she had just heard that one of the men obligated to redeem her family had fed her daughter-in-law from his own table.

Ruth stayed in Boaz's fields through the rest of the barley harvest and the wheat harvest after it, weeks of steady provision, working alongside his servant girls as Naomi advised: "My daughter, it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field." Nothing dramatic happened in those weeks, and the book does not rush past them. A widow was fed, a foreigner was safe, and an old woman at home was doing arithmetic again, but a different kind than on the road to Bethlehem. Naomi had a redeemer in view now, and a daughter-in-law of noble character, and the harvest was ending.

title: Under His Wings
subtitle: Ruth 3 to 4
description: A midnight proposal, a morning at the gate, and a baby who changes the genealogy.
paragraphs: The harvests ended, and Naomi, who had spent the road home telling her daughters-in-law to find their future somewhere else, began to build one herself. "My daughter, should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?" Resting place is the very thing she had prayed God would give Ruth in a new husband's house back in chapter 1. The blessing had not been answered in Moab or on the road. Naomi had decided, apparently, to become part of its answer, and her instrument was the fact she had filed away the night Ruth came home with an ephah of barley: Boaz was a kinsman-redeemer, and tonight he would be winnowing barley on the threshing floor.

Her instructions were precise and they were daring. "Therefore wash yourself, put on perfume, and wear your best clothes. Go down to the threshing floor, but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking. When he lies down, note the place where he lies. Then go in and uncover his feet, and lie down, and he will explain to you what you should do." Read it plainly: a young foreign widow was to go alone at night to where a wealthy older man slept after his harvest meal, and lie down at his feet, and trust everything to his character. By every custom of that world, Naomi was staking Ruth's reputation, the only asset Ruth had built in Bethlehem, on the proposition that Boaz was exactly what his introduction claimed, a man of noble character. Ruth's answer accepted the whole risk in six words' worth of obedience: "I will do everything you say," she answered.

She did it exactly. Boaz ate and drank and was in good spirits, the text says, using the same word for his heart's gladness that Naomi had used for Ruth's future welfare, and lay down at the end of the heap of grain to sleep beside his harvest, as owners did in threshing season to guard it. Ruth came secretly, uncovered his feet, and lay down. At midnight the cold on his feet or the presence beside them startled him awake, and he turned and found a woman lying there, and asked who she was. Her answer was not an apology and it was not small talk. "I am your servant Ruth," she replied. "Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer."

In Hebrew, the corner of a garment is a kanaf, a wing. It is the same word Boaz himself had used in his prayer over her in the field, that she had come to take refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. Ruth had taken his blessing and turned it into a proposal, in the language of the law: spread your wing over me, marry me, redeem this family, because that office is yours. Everything Naomi's plan risked was now in the open, and everything depended on how this man answered a vulnerable woman in the dark, with no witnesses, when no one would have known.

He answered with a blessing, and with the book's great word for the third and last time: "May the LORD bless you, my daughter. You have shown more kindness now than before, because you have not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor." Kindness, hesed. Her first kindness, Boaz said, was the loyalty she had shown Naomi. This second one was greater: she had not gone shopping for a young husband, rich or poor, but had come to the family's redeemer to raise up the dead man's house. And then he gave her the compliment the narrator had been saving since his own introduction: "And now do not be afraid, my daughter. I will do for you whatever you request, since all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character." A man of noble character, a woman of noble character. The book's two leads carry the same description in the same Hebrew words, and each of them applies it to the other.

Then Boaz did the thing that separates noble character from a romantic gesture. There was a redeemer nearer than he was, and the right was that man's first, and Boaz would not step around the law in the dark even though the law might cost him Ruth. He swore it with an oath: "if he wants to redeem you, good. Let him redeem you. But if he does not want to redeem you, as surely as the LORD lives, I will." She lay at his feet until morning and left before anyone could recognize her, to protect the name she had just been praised for, and he filled her shawl with six measures of barley and sent her home with a sentence Ruth carried back like a report: "Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed." Empty. It was the word Naomi had hurled at heaven in the town square, I went away full and the LORD has brought me back empty, and whether or not Boaz had ever heard that speech, the book sets his sentence against hers and lets them rhyme. Naomi heard the barley hit the floor and the report of the night and delivered her verdict on Boaz, which is also the book's: "Wait, my daughter," said Naomi, "until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today."

He did not rest. That morning Boaz went up to the town gate, where Israel did its legal business, and sat down, and the nearer redeemer happened along, in this book's familiar way of happening, and Boaz seated him and ten elders of the city as witnesses. Then he conducted the negotiation like the careful man he was: land first. Naomi was selling the piece of land that had belonged to Elimelech, and the right to buy it back into the family was the nearer man's before it was Boaz's. "I will redeem it," he replied. Then Boaz laid the rest of it on the table, in public, where it belonged: "On the day you buy the land from Naomi and also from Ruth the Moabitess, you must also acquire the widow of the deceased in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance." The land came with a Moabite widow, and any son she bore would be counted the dead man's heir, inheriting the very land the redeemer had just paid for. The nearer man did his arithmetic in front of the elders and declined: "I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption, because I cannot redeem it." He would not risk his own name to raise up another man's, and the book, which names shepherds and gleaners and towns-women, never gives him a name at all.

An old custom sealed it. The narrator pauses to explain it for readers of a later day, because it was already going out of use: "Now in former times in Israel, concerning the redemption or exchange of property, to make any matter legally binding a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party, and this was a confirmation in Israel." The sandal came off and passed over, and then Boaz stood and made his declaration to the elders and everyone at the gate: "You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon. Moreover, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home. You are witnesses today."

The town answered with a blessing, and listen to whose names Bethlehem reached for to bless a Moabite bride: "May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem. And may your house become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman." Rachel and Leah, the mothers of the nation. And Perez, the son of Tamar, the other widow in this family's history who had to secure the line of Judah by bold action when the men would not. The elders at the gate were blessing Ruth with the two most honored comparisons their family story owned, and one of them was a woman every bit as much an outsider to the line as Ruth herself.

"So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And when he had relations with her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son." There is the book's second direct act of God, set like a clasp opposite the first. In chapter 1 He attended to His people by providing them with food. Here He enables a widow who had been ten years married without a child to conceive. Between those two acts, everything was hesed, people being kind at cost to themselves: a daughter-in-law who would not leave, a landowner who dropped grain on purpose, an old woman who schemed for someone else's future, a redeemer who would not cut a legal corner. The book seems determined to show heaven working almost entirely through that.

And the frame closes exactly where it opened, on Naomi. The women of Bethlehem, the same women who had asked can this be Naomi, now sang over her: "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer. May his name become famous in Israel. He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth." Better than seven sons, the perfect family's number, and it is said of the Moabite. Naomi took the child onto her lap and became his nurse, and the neighbors named him, and what they said is the book in one sentence: "A son has been born to Naomi," they said, and they named him Obed, which means servant. The woman who came home empty holds the future in her lap, and the whole town assigns the baby to her account.

Then the book ends with ten names, and they are not filler, they are the destination. Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, fathered Hezron. Hezron fathered Ram, and Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, the same Nahshon who led the tribe of Judah in the wilderness generation, and Nahshon fathered Salmon, and Salmon fathered Boaz, and Boaz fathered Obed, and Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. David. The genealogy carries the family straight out of Egypt's generation into Bethlehem's greatest house, and it runs, openly and on the record, through a Moabite widow who clung to her mother-in-law on a road. Israel's law in Deuteronomy had said that no Moabite was to enter the assembly of the LORD, even to the tenth generation. Ruth does not argue with that text and does not explain it. It simply lets the names stand where they fall, three generations from Ruth to Israel's king, and closes.

So the judges era, which this series has watched spiral from Gideon to Gibeah, contains this too, in the same years and the same hills: a famine survived, a vow kept, a field gleaned, a gate honored, a baby on an old woman's lap. Everyone in the book does what is right, and almost none of it is in their own eyes. The next story in the order picks up at the tabernacle in Shiloh, where another woman is about to pour out a grief like Naomi's before a priest who does not understand her, and her name is Hannah, and she is praying for a son.
